books.title: In the Mountains
books.art_why: The book shows real animals that live in the mountains today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: The small striped chipmunk lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A small striped chipmunk is shown in the mountains. Its little body stays close to the ground, with clear stripes along its back. The mountain setting rises around it, and the chipmunk looks alert as it lives there.

pages.text: Yes, the small gray squirrel lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A small gray squirrel is shown in the mountains. It sits upright with its gray fur and bushy tail visible. The mountain ground and rising slopes are around it as the squirrel lives in this high place.

pages.text: Yes, the small furry rabbit lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A small furry rabbit is shown in the mountains. Its soft fur and small body are clear as it sits on the mountain ground. The high mountain setting surrounds the rabbit where it lives.

pages.text: Yes, the small sly fox lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A small sly fox is shown in the mountains. Its pointed face and sleek body are visible as it stands on the mountain ground. The mountain setting rises behind the fox where it lives.

pages.text: Yes, the big strong eagle lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A big strong eagle is shown in the mountains. Its large wings and strong body are clear against the mountain setting. The eagle appears powerful as it lives in this high, open place.

pages.text: Yes, the big proud deer lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A big proud deer is shown in the mountains. Its tall body and proud stance are clear on the mountain ground. The high mountain setting rises around the deer where it lives.

pages.text: Yes, the big hungry bear lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A big hungry bear is shown in the mountains. Its large body and hungry look are clear as it stands on the mountain ground. The mountain setting surrounds the bear where it lives.

pages.text: Yes, many animals live in the mountains. Can you name these animals that live in the mountains?
pages.brief: Many mountain animals are shown together in the mountains: a striped chipmunk, a gray squirrel, a furry rabbit, a sly fox, a strong eagle, a proud deer and a hungry bear. They are all in the mountain setting where they live.

books.title: Animals, Animals
books.art_why: All the animals shown are real animals living today, so photographs suit every page.

pages.text: There are many kinds of animals. Elk run fast. Elk live in the mountains. Giraffes are tall. Giraffes have spots.
pages.brief: A wide mountain slope where a herd of elk runs fast, legs stretched mid-stride over the rocky ground. Nearby, two tall giraffes stand together, their long necks reaching up and their spotted coats clearly visible against the sky.

pages.text: Elephants are strong. Elephants have long trunks. Camels live in deserts. Camels can go without water for a long time.
pages.brief: A big elephant stands strong on open ground, its long trunk curling down toward the grass. In another scene, a camel walks across a sandy desert with dunes behind it, far from any water, its hump rising above its back.

pages.text: Foxes have bushy tails. Foxes live in holes in the ground. Zebras have stripes. Zebras live in grassy places.
pages.brief: A fox with a thick bushy tail stands at the entrance of a hole in the ground, dark earth around it. Across grassy places, zebras with black and white stripes graze together on the open plain, heads lowered to the grass.

pages.text: Hippos live near water. Hippos have almost no hair. Polar bears live in cold places. Polar bears eat seals. There are many kinds of animals.
pages.brief: A hippo stands half in shallow water near a muddy bank, its smooth skin showing almost no hair. On cold ice and snow, a polar bear holds a seal, the frozen white land stretching away behind it.

books.title: Let's Make Lemonade
books.art_why: Making lemonade with real lemons, water, sugar and a pitcher is an everyday kitchen activity that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Let’s Make Lemonade.
pages.brief: A young boy and a young girl stand together in a bright kitchen, smiling beside a tall clear pitcher and a bowl of fresh yellow lemons on the counter, ready to begin making lemonade on a warm day.

pages.text: It’s so hot today. We’re so thirsty for a cold drink.
pages.brief: Two children sit on the front steps of a house in strong sunshine, fanning their faces and looking hot and tired, both wishing for a cold drink, with the sunny street and warm sky behind them.

pages.text: Let’s make a cold drink. Let’s make a sweet drink.
pages.brief: The two children stand at the kitchen counter talking together, one holding up an empty glass, the other pointing at the lemons and the sugar bowl, planning a cold, sweet drink to cool down.

pages.text: Let’s make lemonade. Let’s make it in this pitcher.
pages.brief: A child holds a large clear glass pitcher steady on the counter while the other child sets fresh yellow lemons and a bag of white sugar beside it, both getting ready to make lemonade in the pitcher.

pages.text: Add cold water. Add white sugar.
pages.brief: Small hands pour cold water from a jug into the clear pitcher, then tip white sugar from a small bowl into the water, the water swirling as the sugar sinks down at the kitchen counter.

pages.text: Roll and cut the lemons. Squeeze the lemons.
pages.brief: A child rolls a lemon firmly under the palm of a hand on the counter, then cuts it into halves and squeezes each half over the pitcher, juice dripping down into the water below.

pages.text: Spot the lemon seeds. Pick out all the seeds!
pages.brief: Close view of children's fingers picking small pale lemon seeds out of the cut lemon halves and off the counter top, dropping the seeds aside so the lemonade stays smooth.

pages.text: Stir the lemonade with a long spoon.
pages.brief: A child holds a long spoon and stirs the lemonade round and round inside the clear pitcher, the sugar dissolving and the juice mixing through the water, with the other child watching closely.

pages.text: Don’t spill the pitcher! Lemonade is sticky.
pages.brief: Two children carry the full pitcher carefully across the kitchen with steady hands and worried faces, keeping it level so nothing sloshes over the edge onto the counter top.

pages.text: Our drink looks cold. Our drink looks sweet.
pages.brief: Two glasses of pale yellow lemonade stand on the counter with droplets of water on the outside, the children looking at them happily, seeing how cold and sweet the drink appears.

pages.text: We’re so thirsty for our lemonade.
pages.brief: The two children sit together holding their glasses of cold lemonade, eyes closed and faces glad as they take long, thirsty drinks after making the lemonade themselves in the kitchen.

books.title: All Kinds of Factories
books.art_why: Factories, machines, robots and materials are real things that exist today, so real photographs fit best.

pages.text: What Is a Factory? Factories are big buildings where goods are made.
pages.brief: A wide photograph of a very large factory building with tall walls, a broad roof and big loading doors. Stacks of finished goods in boxes sit near the doors, showing that this big building is a place where goods are made.

pages.text: Some factories are in the city. Some factories are in the country.
pages.brief: Two views side by side: a factory standing among tall city buildings, busy streets and traffic; and a factory standing in the countryside with open fields, a fence and trees around it under a wide sky.

pages.text: Some factories use huge machines. Some factories use small machines.
pages.brief: Inside a factory, a huge machine towers over the floor with thick pipes and turning parts. Beside it, on a workbench, small machines sit close together, showing the difference in size between them.

pages.text: Some factories have robots make goods. Some factories have people make goods. Some factories have both make goods.
pages.brief: Three scenes across the factory floor: robot arms lifting and fitting goods on one line, people working with their hands at a bench, and a line where robots and people work together making goods side by side.

pages.text: What Do Factories Make? This factory turns wood into paper. People write or draw on paper.
pages.brief: Inside a paper factory, thick wooden logs and wood chips are fed into machinery, and out come wide rolls and flat sheets of smooth white paper stacked and ready to be written and drawn on.

pages.text: This factory turns cotton into cloth. People use cloth to make clothes.
pages.brief: In a cloth factory, bales of fluffy cotton are pulled into machines that spin and weave it, and long rolls of finished cloth come out, ready to be cut and sewn into clothes.

pages.text: This factory turns sand into glass. People use glass in windows.
pages.brief: At a glass factory, piles of sand are heated in a hot furnace, and out come flat, clear panes of glass, stacked and shining, the kind of glass fitted into windows.

pages.text: This factory puts parts together to make cars. People use cars to drive to different places.
pages.brief: On a car factory line, metal parts and panels are fitted and joined together, step by step, until a whole finished car stands complete on the factory floor.

pages.text: What did you use today that came from a factory?
pages.brief: A child sits at a table at home, looking at everyday things spread out in front of them: a cup, a pencil, shoes and a toothbrush, all goods that were made in factories and used during the day.

books.title: What's In That Pouch?
books.art_why: Real animals and nature can be shown in photographs.

pages.text: What’s in That Pouch?
pages.brief: A simple, warm cover-style scene centered on a soft animal pouch, shown partly open in a sunny natural setting. Nothing is visible inside yet, and the image invites a young reader to wonder what might be tucked within.

pages.text: Some animal moms carry the baby in a pouch. The baby rides and sleeps in the pouch. What’s in that pouch? It’s a baby koala! (koh-AW-luh)
pages.brief: An animal mother carries her baby in a pouch, with the baby riding and sleeping snugly inside. The mother is a koala, and the baby koala is tucked in the pouch, resting while the mother carries it.

pages.text: A koala sits in trees. A koala eats leaves. What’s in that pouch? It’s a baby wallaby!
pages.brief: A koala sits high in trees and eats leaves, holding onto the branches. A baby wallaby is tucked inside a pouch, with only its small face and body visible as it rides quietly and safely along.

pages.text: A wallaby lives near the woods. A wallaby eats plants. What’s in that pouch? It’s two baby bilbies!
pages.brief: A wallaby lives near the woods and eats plants, standing at the woodland edge. Two baby bilbies are tucked inside a pouch, with their tiny faces and bodies peeking out together as they ride along.

pages.text: A bilby lives in the desert. A bilby eats bugs and seeds. I’m in my mom’s pouch! I’m a baby kangaroo!
pages.brief: A bilby lives in the desert and eats bugs and seeds on the sandy ground. A baby kangaroo is tucked inside its mom’s pouch, with its head out and mouth open as if speaking happily.

pages.text: A kangaroo hops in the bushes. A kangaroo eats plants. What’s in that pouch? Me! Me! Me! Me! Me!
pages.brief: A kangaroo hops through bushes and eats plants, moving through the green growth. From inside the pouch, a baby kangaroo pops out and calls out loudly and repeatedly, again and again, with a lively, eager expression.

books.title: The First Strawberry
books.art_why: Real strawberries, gardens, and gardening steps can be photographed.

pages.text: Do you love strawberries? Try growing your own!
pages.brief: Ripe red strawberries grow on green strawberry plants, with healthy leaves and bright fruit filling a close view. The image invites the viewer to imagine growing their own strawberries, showing the fruit people love and the plant that produces it.

pages.text: Pick a sunny spot for your strawberry patch in spring.
pages.brief: An open garden spot chosen for a strawberry patch in spring, with bright sunlight falling across the ground and clear space for strawberry plants to grow. The scene shows the warm, sunny conditions needed for a new spring patch.

pages.text: Buy some plants for your strawberry patch.
pages.brief: Young strawberry plants are shown together, ready to be bought for a new patch. Healthy green leaves rise from small pots of dark soil, and several plants sit close together in a simple garden-center display with clear space around them.

pages.text: Plant the plants in your strawberry patch. Leave room for them to spread.
pages.brief: Young strawberry plants are planted in a garden patch, set apart with open soil between them. Each plant has green leaves and sits upright in the soil. The spaces left around the plants show they have room to spread as they grow.

pages.text: Spread straw in your strawberry patch. Straw helps prevent weeds and pests.
pages.brief: A strawberry patch is covered with dry golden straw. The straw is spread around the base of the young plants, covering the soil between them while green leaves remain visible. The layer of straw sits in place to help prevent weeds and pests.

pages.text: Water your strawberry patch at least twice a week.
pages.brief: Water soaks into the soil around young strawberry plants in the patch. Droplets cling to the green leaves, and the ground looks dark and damp. The patch receives a good watering, showing the moisture the plants need at least twice a week.

pages.text: The plants in your strawberry patch will bloom. Then, the plants will make small green fruits.
pages.brief: Strawberry plants in the patch show open white blossoms. Nearby, small green fruits have formed where flowers once were, tucked among green leaves. The plants are moving from bloom to fruit, showing the first small green strawberries.

pages.text: The green fruits in your strawberry patch will turn pale. Then they will turn red.
pages.brief: Green strawberries in the patch are turning pale, then red. Some fruits still look green or pale, while others show bright red color on the plant. The strawberries are ripening among green leaves in the strawberry patch.

pages.text: Pick those fruits in your strawberry patch. Wash and eat them.
pages.brief: Red strawberries are picked into a small basket, then rinsed in a bowl of water. Clean strawberries sit nearby, ready to eat. The scene shows the ripe fruits from the patch being gathered, washed, and prepared for eating.

pages.text: The first strawberry will taste the very best.
pages.brief: One ripe red strawberry sits in clear view, freshly picked and shiny. It looks sweet and inviting, standing out as the very best first strawberry from the patch. The close-up shows the fruit that will taste the best.

books.title: How Many Teeth?
books.art_why: Real animals and a child can be photographed.

pages.text: How Many Teeth?
pages.brief: A bright close-up photo of a human smile with teeth clearly visible, filling the frame, suggesting the question of counting teeth. The mouth is the only subject, with soft lighting and a simple, blurred background.

pages.text: Different animals have different numbers of teeth.
pages.brief: Several different animals are shown together in a simple outdoor scene, each with its mouth open enough to reveal its teeth. The animals stand side by side on open ground, and the setting is plain so their different mouths and teeth are easy to compare.

pages.text: A snake can have two fangs.
pages.brief: A single snake rests on the ground in a natural outdoor setting, its mouth open wide enough to show two sharp fangs. Leaves and small plants surround the snake, and the close view focuses on its head and mouth. No other animals appear.

pages.text: A vampire bat can have twenty teeth.
pages.brief: A vampire bat hangs upside down in a dim cave, its mouth open to reveal twenty small teeth. Its wings are folded close to its body, and rough rock walls fill the background. The bat is the only animal shown, and the view focuses on its face.

pages.text: A horse can have forty teeth.
pages.brief: A single horse stands in an open grassy field, its head turned toward the viewer with its mouth open to show forty teeth. The horse is calm, with a plain pasture and sky behind it, and no other animals or people appear in the scene.

pages.text: An opossum can have fifty teeth.
pages.brief: An opossum perches on a tree branch, its mouth open to show fifty small teeth. Its long snout and bare tail are visible, and green leaves surround it in a woodland setting. The opossum is the only animal in the scene, shown clearly from the side.

pages.text: An alligator can have eighty teeth.
pages.brief: An alligator lies half-submerged in a murky swamp, its long jaws open wide to show rows of eighty teeth. Reeds and still water surround it, and the alligator is the only animal visible. The view is close enough to see its mouth clearly.

pages.text: A sand tiger shark can have ninety-six teeth.
pages.brief: A sand tiger shark swims underwater, facing forward with its mouth open to show rows of ninety-six sharp teeth. Blue water and soft sand surround it, and sunlight filters down from above. The shark is the only animal in the scene.

pages.text: A dolphin can have two hundred fifty teeth.
pages.brief: A dolphin swims in clear blue water, its mouth slightly open to show two hundred fifty small teeth. Its smooth body and fins are visible as it glides forward, and no other animals are nearby. Bright sunlight fills the water around it.

pages.text: A snail can have twenty-five thousand teeth!
pages.brief: A small snail crawls across a green leaf, with a very close view of its mouth area to suggest the huge number of tiny teeth inside. The snail is the only animal shown, and the leaf fills the background.

pages.text: How many teeth do you have?
pages.brief: A young child smiles with an open mouth, showing a full set of teeth, and looks toward the viewer as if inviting them to count. The child stands in a bright, simple room, and no other people or objects are shown.

books.title: Arctic Animals
books.art_why: Arctic animals and places exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Some animals live in cold places. The Arctic is one of the coldest places on Earth.
pages.brief: A wide, frozen Arctic landscape stretching to the horizon, with flat white snow, pale blue sea ice and dark cold water in the distance. Low grey clouds and cold light fill the sky, and a few small animals can be seen far away across the snowy ground.

pages.text: Hares live in the Arctic. They turn white in the winter.
pages.brief: A single Arctic hare sits on snowy ground in a cold, open landscape. Its fur is pure white, matching the snow all around it, with only its dark eyes and nose showing. Small rocks and dry grass poke through the snow nearby under a pale winter sky.

pages.text: Snowy owls live in the Arctic. They hunt in the day.
pages.brief: A snowy owl flies low over a white Arctic field in bright daylight, its white feathers with dark flecks spread wide. Its yellow eyes look down at the snow as it hunts. Behind it are flat snowy ground and a cold, light sky.

pages.text: Foxes live in the Arctic. They have thick fur.
pages.brief: An Arctic fox stands on snow in a cold, open place, its thick white furry coat puffed out around its body and tail. It looks toward the camera with small dark eyes and rounded ears. Snow and ice stretch behind it under a grey sky.

pages.text: Wolves live in the Arctic. They hunt in packs.
pages.brief: A pack of grey and white wolves runs together across a snowy Arctic plain, spread out in a line with their heads low and breath steaming in the cold air. Snow covers the ground and low hills rise in the distance under a pale sky.

pages.text: Caribou live in the Arctic. They are good swimmers.
pages.brief: Several caribou with large branching antlers swim across cold Arctic water, their heads and shaggy backs above the surface. Ripples spread around them as they move forward, with a snowy shore and icy hills visible behind.

pages.text: Moose live in the Arctic. They fight with their antlers.
pages.brief: Two large moose stand facing each other on snowy ground, their huge palmate antlers locked together as they push and fight. Their dark bodies and long legs are braced in the snow, with bare trees and cold sky behind them.

pages.text: Harp seals live in the Arctic. They have white fur as pups.
pages.brief: A harp seal mother lies on white sea ice beside her pup, which is covered in soft, fluffy white fur. The pup rests close to her on the ice, and dark cold water shows at the edge of the ice behind them under a pale sky.

pages.text: Orcas live in the Arctic. They hunt many sea animals.
pages.brief: A black-and-white orca swims through cold dark Arctic water, its tall fin and white patches clear above and below the surface. Fish scatter in the water nearby as it hunts. Pale ice floats on the water in the background under a grey sky.

pages.text: Polar bears live in the Arctic. Moms stay with their cubs for years.
pages.brief: A large polar bear mother stands on snowy ice with her small cubs close beside her, their white fur blending with the snow. The mother watches over them as they walk together across the ice, with cold sea and floating ice behind.

books.title: City Animals
books.art_why: City animals and places are real and can be photographed today.

pages.text: Many people live in cities. Many kinds of animals live in cities, too. Mice live in cities. They eat food people throw away.
pages.brief: A city place shows many people living there, and many kinds of animals living there too. Several mice are in the city, eating food that people have thrown away. The mice stay near the discarded food in the city.

pages.text: Geese and ducks live in cities. They swim in ponds in parks. Squirrels live in cities. Squirrels make nests in trees.
pages.brief: A park pond in a city shows geese and ducks swimming on the water. Nearby, squirrels live in the city and make nests in trees. The geese and ducks are in the pond, while the squirrels are in the trees with their nests.

pages.text: Pigeons live in cities. Some people like to feed pigeons. Opossums live in cities. They like to come out at night.
pages.brief: In a city place, pigeons are shown as people feed them. Later, at night, an opossum comes out in the city. The picture shows pigeons with people feeding them, and an opossum out at night in the city.

pages.text: Hawks live in cities. They make nests on tall buildings. Dogs live in cities. People bring them to the park.
pages.brief: A tall city building shows a hawk making a nest on it. In a city park, people bring dogs. The hawk is on the tall building with its nest, while dogs and people are together in the park.

pages.text: Raccoons live in cities. They take food from trash bins. Do you see animals where you live? What kinds of animals do you see?
pages.brief: Raccoons are in a city, taking food from trash bins. The scene shows the raccoons at the trash bins as they get food. The city around them is a place where people live and animals can be seen.

books.title: Spending Dimes One at a Time
books.art_why: Real-world store, coins and toys can be photographed.

pages.text: At the store, a sign says that each item costs one dime. I have ten dimes. I spend one dime. Now the ball is mine.
pages.brief: At a store, a young child holds ten dimes and hands one dime over to buy a ball. The new ball is now in the child's hands, and a store price sign stands nearby at the shop.

pages.text: How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: At the store, a young child looks down at a handful of dimes and pauses quietly, thinking about how many dimes are left. The child's open hands and the dimes are the main focus in the scene.

pages.text: I have nine dimes. I spend one dime. Now the tiger is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: A young child at the store holds nine dimes and hands one dime over to buy a toy tiger. The child now holds the tiger and looks at the remaining dimes, wondering how many are left.

pages.text: I have eight dimes. I spend one dime. Now the whistle is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: A young child at the store holds eight dimes and hands one dime over to buy a whistle. The child now holds the whistle and looks at the remaining dimes, wondering how many dimes are left.

pages.text: I have seven dimes. I spend one dime. Now the robot is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: A young child at the store holds seven dimes and hands one dime over to buy a robot toy. The child now holds the robot and looks at the remaining dimes, wondering how many dimes are left.

pages.text: I have six dimes. I spend one dime. Now the puppet is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: A young child at the store holds six dimes and hands one dime over to buy a puppet. The child now holds the puppet and looks at the remaining dimes, wondering how many dimes are left.

pages.text: I have five dimes. I spend one dime. Now the airplane is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: A young child at the store holds five dimes and hands one dime over to buy an airplane toy. The child now holds the airplane and looks at the remaining dimes, wondering how many dimes are left.

pages.text: I have four dimes. I spend one dime. Now the turtle is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: A young child at the store holds four dimes and hands one dime over to buy a turtle toy. The child now holds the turtle and looks at the remaining dimes, wondering how many dimes are left.

pages.text: I have three dimes. I spend one dime. Now the sticker is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: A young child at the store holds three dimes and hands one dime over to buy a sticker. The child now holds the sticker and looks at the remaining dimes, wondering how many dimes are left.

pages.text: I have two dimes. I spend one dime. Now the key chain is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: A young child at the store holds two dimes and hands one dime over to buy a key chain. The child now holds the key chain and looks at the remaining dimes, wondering how many dimes are left.

pages.text: I have one dime. I spend one dime. Now the shell is mine. I have zero dimes, but I have ten items!
pages.brief: A young child holds one last dime and hands it over to buy a shell. The child now has zero dimes and stands with ten small items gathered together, including the shell and the toys bought before.

books.title: Caring For Earth
books.art_why: Real children, gardens, bikes, animals and recycling can be photographed today.

pages.text: How can we help take care of Earth? We care for Earth when we tend gardens.
pages.brief: Children kneel in a sunny garden bed, gently tending rows of green plants. One child loosens the soil around the stems while another carefully supports the leaves. Their hands work close to the ground as they tend the garden together.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we plant new trees.
pages.brief: Two children plant a young tree in a cleared patch of soil outdoors. One child holds the slender sapling upright while the other pats soil around its base, helping the new tree settle into the ground.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we reuse things.
pages.brief: Children sit at a table with everyday items they are using again. They sort empty containers and boxes, setting them aside for another purpose instead of throwing them away, showing how reusing things helps care for Earth.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we recycle.
pages.brief: Children place empty cans and paper into recycling bins outdoors. One child lifts a can toward the open bin while another carries a stack of paper, sorting materials so they can be recycled instead of thrown away.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we ride our bikes to school.
pages.brief: Children ride bicycles along a path toward a school building. They pedal in a small group, moving together on their bikes for the trip to school, showing one way to care for Earth. The school is visible ahead.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we use less water.
pages.brief: A child stands at a sink and turns the tap off while washing hands. Water drips stop as the tap closes, and the child uses only a small amount, showing how using less water helps care for Earth.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we save electricity.
pages.brief: A child reaches up to switch off a light in a bright room. The room is lit by daylight from a window, and the child turns off the unnecessary light, showing how saving electricity helps care for Earth.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we help animals.
pages.brief: A child gently helps a small animal outdoors, offering it food and water in a safe, quiet spot. The child moves slowly and calmly, caring for the animal without startling it, showing one way people can help animals.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we clean up trash outdoors.
pages.brief: Children clean up trash outdoors in an open area. They wear gloves and carry bags, bending to pick up litter from the grass and path, working together to leave the outdoor place cleaner and safer for everyone.

pages.text: We can care for Earth in many different ways. Our care can make a big difference.
pages.brief: A group of children stand together outdoors, each showing a different caring action: tending a garden, planting a young tree, riding a bike, recycling, and cleaning up. Their shared effort shows that many small actions can make a big difference for Earth.

books.title: Crazy Cakes
books.art_why: Real cakes and cake artists exist today, so photographs are possible.

pages.text: Some artists use paint or marble to make their art. Other artists use cake and frosting!
pages.brief: An artist decorates a cake with frosting, showing that cake and frosting can be art materials just like paint or marble. The cake sits in front of the artist as they pipe frosting onto it.

pages.text: Some of their cakes just look pretty. Other cakes look like something else.
pages.brief: Some cakes are shown looking only pretty, while other cakes are shown looking like something else entirely. The picture presents both kinds of cake together, so a pretty cake can be seen next to a cake that looks like another object.

pages.text: This cake looks like a pretty peacock.
pages.brief: A cake is decorated to look like a pretty peacock. The cake's shape and frosting create the peacock's body, feathers, and head, so the whole cake reads as a beautiful bird rather than a dessert.

pages.text: This cake looks like a giant rooster.
pages.brief: A cake is made to look like a giant rooster. The cake's form and frosting clearly shape the rooster's body and head, making the large bird stand out as a playful cake creation on display.

pages.text: This cake looks like a fancy crown.
pages.brief: A cake is decorated to look like a fancy crown. The cake's frosting and shape form the crown's points and band, so the whole finished dessert appears as a royal headpiece made of cake.

pages.text: This cake looks like a fish and hook.
pages.brief: A cake is shaped to look like a fish and a hook. The cake's frosting and form clearly create the fish's body and the curved hook, making the whole small cake resemble a fishing catch.

pages.text: This cake looks like a busy beehive.
pages.brief: A cake is decorated to look like a busy beehive. The cake's rounded shape and frosting create the hive, with small details suggesting bees around it, so the whole dessert appears as a lively hive.

pages.text: This cake looks like a treasure chest.
pages.brief: A cake is shaped to look like a treasure chest. The cake's frosting and form clearly create the chest's lid and sides, making the whole small finished dessert resemble a closed chest full of treasure.

pages.text: This cake looks like a magic unicorn.
pages.brief: A cake is decorated to look like a magic unicorn. The cake's frosting and shape clearly create the unicorn's head, horn, and mane, so the whole dessert appears as a magical creature made of cake.

pages.text: These cakes look almost too good to eat. They taste as good as they look!
pages.brief: Several finished cakes are clearly displayed together, looking almost too good to eat. All the cakes in the whole group are shown as very beautiful creations that also taste just as good as they look.

books.title: Sew Who?
books.art_why: A real felt-craft project with real hands, felt, pins, stuffing and a finished sewn owl, all things that exist and can be photographed today.

pages.text: Are you ready to make an owl? Here is what you need to get started. Cut two body shapes from brown felt.
pages.brief: Hands work at a table laid out with brown felt, scissors, needle and thread. The hands cut two owl body shapes from the brown felt, both the same rounded shape, with the finished cut pieces lying beside the leftover felt scraps.

pages.text: Cut two eyes and one belly from white felt. Cut two wings and one beak from orange felt. Pin the eyes on one of the body shapes. Sew them in place.
pages.brief: Two white felt eyes and one white belly lie cut out, next to two orange wings and one orange beak. Hands pin the two eyes onto one brown body shape and sew them in place with needle and thread.

pages.text: Pin the beak under the eyes. Sew it in place. Pin the belly under the beak. Sew it in place.
pages.brief: The brown body shape now holds the sewn white eyes. Hands pin the orange beak just under the eyes and sew it down, then pin the white belly below the beak and sew that in place too.

pages.text: Pin the wings and sew them in place. Pin and sew the two body shapes almost together. Place stuffing inside.
pages.brief: Hands pin the two orange wings to the sides of the brown body and sew them on. The two brown body shapes are pinned almost together, and stuffing is pushed inside through the small gap left open.

pages.text: Sew the two body shapes all the way together. Use markers to finish your owl.
pages.brief: The finished felt owl sits on the table, the two brown body shapes now sewn all the way together and plump with stuffing. Hands hold markers and add the last details to the owl's face.

books.title: Which Tree?
books.art_why: Real trees and leaves exist today, so photographs fit best.

pages.text: You can tell trees by their leaves.
pages.brief: A close view of several different leaves on branches, each leaf a different shape and edge, with the trunks of several trees standing behind them in a green woodland. The leaves are spread out side by side so their differences are clear.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree can be hollow inside.
pages.brief: A tree with a wide hollow opening in its trunk stands in a leafy woodland. Its own leaves fill the lower branches in the foreground, and the dark hollow inside the trunk is clearly visible behind them.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree has a sharp trunk.
pages.brief: A tree trunk covered in sharp, pointed spines rises among green leaves. The tree’s leaves hang close to the spiky trunk in the foreground, showing the sharp surface along the bark and the pointed spines.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree makes sweet syrup.
pages.brief: A tree with broad green leaves stands in a sunny woodland. A glossy drip of sweet syrup runs down the bark of its trunk, and the leaves spread above it, showing the tree that makes syrup.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree has many colors.
pages.brief: A tree with leaves in many bright colors—red, orange, yellow, and green—stands in a woodland. The colorful leaves fill the wide branches and spread across the canopy, showing many colors on one tree.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree looks like an umbrella.
pages.brief: A tree with a wide, rounded canopy shaped like an open umbrella stands in a green woodland. Its tall leafy branches cover the umbrella-like shape, and the trunk rises straight beneath the broad, curved top.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree is the tallest.
pages.brief: A very tall tree with a high canopy of leaves rises above the other trees in a woodland. Its trunk stretches upward, and the leaves are far above, showing the tallest tree in the scene.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree is covered in fruit.
pages.brief: A tree with green leaves and many bright round fruits hanging from its branches stands in a woodland. The fruit is clustered among the leaves, covering the branches so the tree looks full of fruit.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree grows roots from branches.
pages.brief: A tree with green leaves and many long roots hanging down from its branches stands in a clear woodland. The roots drop from the branches toward the ground, hanging among the leaves and the trunk.

pages.text: All trees have their own special leaves. All leaves have their own special trees!
pages.brief: A group of different trees stands together in a woodland, each with its own special leaves. Their leaves vary in shape and color, and the trees rise side by side, showing that every leaf belongs to its own tree.

books.title: All About Orcas
books.art_why: Orcas are real ocean animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Orcas are mammals. They are big dolphins.
pages.brief: A large orca swims through open blue seawater, its black back and white belly clearly visible, rounded head breaking the surface light. In the distance a second orca moves beside it, showing the two animals travelling together as a small group in the ocean.

pages.text: Orcas live in the ocean. They live in cold water.
pages.brief: Wide view of a cold grey ocean under a pale sky, small waves and mist over the water. Two orcas surface in the chilly sea, their dorsal fins cutting the surface, one close to the front and one further back near drifting ice.

pages.text: Orcas breathe air. They breathe through a blowhole.
pages.brief: Close view of an orca at the water surface, its blowhole open on top of its head as a tall misty spray of water and air shoots upward. Around it the sea is calm and bright, with the orca's dark head above the surface.

pages.text: Orcas are black and white. Their color helps them hide in the water.
pages.brief: An orca swims just below the surface, its black back and white patches blending with the shifting light and shadow of the water. Seen from above, the pattern of black and white makes the animal hard to pick out against the moving sea.

pages.text: Orcas are called “killer whales.” They are strong hunters.
pages.brief: A strong orca surges forward through the ocean, mouth slightly open, hunting in open water. Its heavy body and big fins show its power as it moves fast, leaving a swirl of white water behind it near the surface.

pages.text: Orcas are also called “wolves of the sea.” They hunt in packs.
pages.brief: Three orcas hunt together in a group, spread across the water in a loose line, fins breaking the surface as they move in the same direction. The sea around them is cold and deep, showing the animals working as a pack.

pages.text: Orcas have big teeth. They do not chew their food.
pages.brief: Close-up of an orca's head with its mouth open, showing a row of large sharp teeth along the jaw. The dark eye and white chin patch are visible against the water, and a whole fish is held near the teeth.

pages.text: Orcas eat other sea animals. They hunt fish, seals, and even other dolphins.
pages.brief: An orca chases fish in the ocean, silver fish scattering in a bright shoal ahead of its open mouth. Farther off, a seal swims near the surface and another dolphin moves past, all in cold blue water.

pages.text: Orcas have big fins. Fins help them move through the water.
pages.brief: Side view of an orca swimming, its large dorsal fin tall on its back and wide flippers out to the sides. The fins push through the blue water as the animal glides forward, leaving a smooth wake.

pages.text: Orcas are powerful ocean animals.
pages.brief: A powerful orca swims alone through deep blue ocean, strong body and big fins clear in the light from above. The water stretches away in every direction, showing a big, strong animal at home in the open sea.

books.title: Food Trucks
books.art_why: Food trucks, people and food are real-world subjects that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Food trucks are trucks where people make and sell food.
pages.brief: A food truck parked in an open outdoor spot, with people inside the truck making food at a counter and selling it through the truck's open side. The truck is the main focus, showing it is a truck used for food.

pages.text: Each food truck has a kitchen inside.
pages.brief: Inside a food truck, a small kitchen area is shown, with people working within the truck's interior. The view makes clear that the kitchen is built inside the food truck, fitting into the compact space where food is made.

pages.text: This food truck sells fish and chips. This food truck sells barbecue.
pages.brief: Two food trucks are parked side by side outdoors. One truck shows fish and chips being sold, and the other truck shows barbecue being sold. The trucks are the focus, with their food offerings visible at each truck.

pages.text: This food truck sells chicken. This food truck sells pizza.
pages.brief: Two food trucks are parked side by side outdoors. One truck is shown selling chicken, and the other truck is shown selling pizza. The two trucks stand as the main subject, making clear that each truck sells a different kind of food.

pages.text: This food truck sells Indian food. This food truck sells Japanese food.
pages.brief: Two food trucks are parked side by side outdoors. One truck is shown selling Indian food, and the other truck is shown selling Japanese food. The trucks are the main subject, showing two different kinds of food being sold from food trucks.

pages.text: This food truck sells hot dogs. This food truck sells grilled cheese sandwiches.
pages.brief: Two food trucks are parked side by side outdoors. One truck is shown selling hot dogs, and the other truck is shown selling grilled cheese sandwiches. The trucks are the main subject, with each truck offering its own food.

pages.text: This food truck sells seafood. This food truck sells tacos.
pages.brief: Two food trucks are parked side by side outdoors. One truck is shown selling seafood, and the other truck is shown selling tacos. The trucks are the main subject, making clear that each food truck sells a different kind of food.

pages.text: This food truck sells ribs. This food truck sells hamburgers.
pages.brief: Two food trucks are parked side by side outdoors. One truck is shown selling ribs, and the other truck is shown selling hamburgers. The trucks are the main subject, showing two different foods sold from food trucks.

pages.text: Food trucks go wherever there are crowds of people.
pages.brief: Several food trucks are parked near a large crowd of people gathered outdoors. The trucks are set up where the people are, showing that food trucks go wherever crowds gather. People stand around the trucks in a busy outdoor setting.

pages.text: The food can taste really good!
pages.brief: A close view of freshly made food from a food truck, looking hot and delicious. The food is shown as the main subject, with appealing color and texture that suggest it can taste really good. A food truck is visible softly in the background.

books.title: Goodbye Snow
books.art_why: Snow, shovels, snowplows and dump trucks all exist today and can be photographed in real life.

pages.text: Some places get a lot of snow.
pages.brief: A wide photo of a snowy neighbourhood after a heavy snowfall. Deep white snow covers the roofs of small houses, the fences, the parked cars and the street, with snow still piled high on the branches of the trees.

pages.text: When snow gets in the way, it must be removed. There are many ways to remove snow.
pages.brief: A street where thick snow blocks the way, covering the pavement and the road. Shovels, a stiff brush, a snowblower and a plow truck wait nearby in the cleared area, ready to be used to clear the snow away.

pages.text: Snow can be removed with a shovel.
pages.brief: A person in a warm winter coat, hat and gloves holds a wide shovel and pushes it along a snowy garden path, lifting the white snow into a pile at the side so the path becomes clear.

pages.text: Snow can be removed with a brush.
pages.brief: Close view of hands in thick gloves holding a stiff brush, sweeping soft snow off a car windscreen and the top of a garden wall, leaving clean clear surfaces behind in the cold winter air.

pages.text: Snow can be removed with a snowblower.
pages.brief: A person grips a snowblower and walks it along a snowy driveway. The machine throws a high white arc of snow out of a chute to the side, clearing a wide path across the drive.

pages.text: Snow can be removed with a snowplow.
pages.brief: A big snowplow truck drives along a snowy road, its wide blade pushing a heavy roll of white snow ahead of it and off to the side of the street, leaving cleared road behind.

pages.text: Snow can be removed with salt.
pages.brief: A worker in winter clothing scatters salt from a bucket or spreader over an icy, snowy stretch of pavement. Small white grains land on the ice and the wet surface begins to clear.

pages.text: Snow can be removed with a snow melter.
pages.brief: A large snow melter machine sits on a snowy street, taking in loads of snow and letting out warm water. Steam rises from the machine into the cold air while a truck waits close by.

pages.text: Dump trucks may take snow away.
pages.brief: A dump truck parked beside a snowy road, its big open bed filled with heap after heap of white snow. A loader lifts more snow and drops it into the back of the truck.

pages.text: Where does a dump truck take snow? A snow dump!
pages.brief: A dump truck tips up its bed and empties a huge load of snow onto a wide open snow dump, a great white field of piled snow stretching away in the winter light.

books.title: Alive with Light
books.art_why: Bioluminescent animals and their glowing light exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Alive with Light.
pages.brief: A dark night scene filled with small glowing creatures: tiny lights in blue, yellow, red and green shine against black water and black air, showing living things that are alive with light.

pages.text: Alive with.
pages.brief: A close view of a single glowing creature in the dark, its soft light spreading into the black around it, with more faint points of light from other living things far behind it.

pages.text: Light helps animals see the world around them. It’s hard to see things where there is not much light.
pages.brief: An animal in a dim place looking toward its surroundings, with a dark, shadowy area beside it where shapes are hard to make out, showing how light helps animals see the world around them.

pages.text: Some living things can make light on their own.
pages.brief: A small living thing in the dark giving off its own light from its body, glowing brightly while the space around it stays black, showing a living thing that makes light on its own.

pages.text: Some living things make blue light.
pages.brief: Tiny living things in dark water glowing bright blue, their blue light spreading through the water around them while the rest of the scene stays deep and black.

pages.text: Some living things make yellow light.
pages.brief: Small flying insects in the night air glowing warm yellow, each one a soft yellow point of light against the dark trees and dark sky behind them.

pages.text: Some living things make red light.
pages.brief: A living thing in deep, dark water giving off a red glow from its body, the red light shining out while everything around it stays black and unseen.

pages.text: Living things can make green light, too.
pages.brief: Living things glowing green in a dark cave or dark water, their green light clinging to the rock and shining in the blackness around them.

pages.text: The light can help living things catch their food.
pages.brief: A deep-sea fish in the dark with a glowing light near its mouth, the bright light shining in black water to help it catch its food.

pages.text: The light can help living things find their mates.
pages.brief: Glowing insects in the night air signalling with their light, two of them shining toward each other in the darkness to help them find their mates.

pages.text: The light can help protect living things so they stay safe.
pages.brief: A small sea creature in dark water releasing a cloud of glowing light around itself, the bright cloud hiding it so it stays safe from a larger animal nearby.

pages.text: People don’t have bodies that give off light. People can enjoy seeing other things alive with light!
pages.brief: People standing outside at night, faces turned up and watching glowing insects and glowing creatures shine in the dark around them, enjoying other things alive with light.

books.title: City Places
books.art_why: City places like parks, stores and stadiums exist today and can be photographed as they really are.

pages.text: There are many places in the city. Let’s find out what some of them are. What is this place? It is a park. People come here to have fun.
pages.brief: A sunny city park filled with people having fun: children running across green grass, a family sitting on a bench, a woman walking a dog along a path, and tall city buildings standing behind the trees at the edge of the park.

pages.text: What is this place? It is a store. People come here to shop. What is this place? It is a zoo. People come here to see animals.
pages.brief: Two city scenes side by side: first a bright store where people shop, pushing carts and carrying baskets between shelves of goods; then a zoo where visitors stand at a railing watching animals in a grassy enclosure under open sky.

pages.text: What is this place? It is a skyscraper. Office workers come here to work. What is this place? It is a stadium. Players come here to play ball.
pages.brief: A tall glass skyscraper rising over the city, office workers in suits walking in through the front doors; beside it a stadium where players in team uniforms run and kick a ball on the field while goalposts stand at each end.

pages.text: What is this place? It is a parking garage. People come here to park their cars. People do many different things in many places in the city. What do you do in the city?
pages.brief: A city parking garage with several levels, cars parked neatly in painted spaces and a driver stepping out of an open car door; beyond the garage walls, city buildings and busy streets full of people doing different things.

books.title: All Kinds of Farms
books.art_why: Farms, animals, crops, and food are real-world subjects that photographs can show clearly.

pages.text: What Lives on Farms? Cows live on farms. Milk comes from cows. People drink milk.
pages.brief: On a dairy farm, several cows stand and graze in a green field while other cows rest nearby. A person pours fresh milk into a glass and drinks it, showing that milk comes from cows on the farm.

pages.text: People make cheese and butter from milk.
pages.brief: On a farm, people make cheese and butter from fresh milk. One person stirs milk in a large pot, while another shapes cheese and packs butter. The finished cheese and butter sit nearby, ready to use.

pages.text: Sheep live on farms. Wool comes from sheep. People make clothes from wool.
pages.brief: On a farm, sheep with thick wool stand in a grassy field. Nearby, people show mittens, a scarf, and a sweater made from sheep wool. The warm clothes are displayed together, showing how wool becomes clothing.

pages.text: Chickens live on farms. Eggs come from chickens. People eat eggs for breakfast.
pages.brief: On a chicken farm, chickens peck around a yard and sit near nests with eggs. A person gathers eggs into a basket, then serves eggs for breakfast on a plate. The eggs come from the chickens on the farm.

pages.text: What Grows on Farms? Apples grow on farms. People eat apples.
pages.brief: In an apple orchard, apple trees are full of red apples. A person reaches up and picks an apple from a branch. A basket of apples sits nearby, and a child eats an apple, showing that people eat apples from farms.

pages.text: Other fruits grow on farms, too. People eat fruits. strawberry plant strawberry jam.
pages.brief: In a fruit orchard, an orange tree holds ripe oranges, and a strawberry plant has red strawberries. A glass of orange juice and a jar of strawberry jam sit nearby. People eat the fruits, which grow on farms.

pages.text: Sugarcane grows on farms. Sugar comes from sugarcane. Sugar makes foods sweet. sugarcane farm sugar.
pages.brief: On a sugarcane farm, tall sugarcane plants grow in rows. Nearby, sugar is shown with pieces of candy, and a person holds a sweet candy. The sugarcane and sugar show how sugar makes foods sweet.

pages.text: Cotton grows on farms. People use cotton to make clothing. Shirts, pants, and socks are made from cotton.
pages.brief: On a cotton farm, cotton plants with white fluffy bolls grow in a field. Nearby, shirts, pants, and socks are shown together. People use cotton to make clothing, and the cotton from the farm becomes the clothes.

pages.text: What did you use today that came from a farm?
pages.brief: A collection of farm products sits together: fruits, juice, cotton shirts, wool sweaters, butter, cheese, vegetables, and milk. These items are shown as things that came from a farm, ready for someone to use today.

books.title: The Four Seasons
books.art_why: Real-world seasons, weather and children can be photographed.

pages.text: There are four seasons.
pages.brief: A wide outdoor landscape is shown in four different seasonal versions at once, each version with its own weather and light, so a viewer can clearly see that there are four seasons in a year.

pages.text: In spring, the rain falls. Children play in the puddles.
pages.brief: In spring, rain falls from the sky onto an outdoor place, and children play in puddles on the ground, splashing and enjoying the wet weather together. The scene shows the rainy spring day and the children's playful fun.

pages.text: The days get longer. Summer comes.
pages.brief: The days get longer as summer comes; a bright outdoor view shows more daylight and a warm sky, making the change from spring to summer easy to see. The scene is open and sunlit, with the longer day clearly felt in the light around the landscape.

pages.text: In summer, the days are hot. Children play at the beach.
pages.brief: In summer, the days are hot, and children play at the beach, enjoying the warm weather by the sand and water in a bright, sunny outdoor setting. The children are shown having fun together on the beach during the hot summer day.

pages.text: It starts to cool off. Fall comes.
pages.brief: The outdoor air starts to cool off as fall arrives; the scene shifts from summer heat to a cooler feeling, showing the change in the weather and the coming of fall. No summer heat is shown now, only a cooler outdoor setting as the new season begins.

pages.text: In fall, trees lose their leaves. Children make faces on pumpkins.
pages.brief: In an autumn setting, trees lose their leaves, and children make faces on pumpkins. Falling and fallen leaves appear around the trees while the children work on the pumpkins, showing the fall season clearly. The scene brings the trees and pumpkins together.

pages.text: The winds get colder. Winter comes.
pages.brief: The winds get colder as winter comes; a chilly outdoor view shows the colder air and wind moving through the landscape, marking the change from fall to winter. The scene feels cold, with the coming winter clear in the moving air and colder wind.

pages.text: In winter, the days are shorter. Children play in the snow.
pages.brief: In winter, the days are shorter, and children play in the snow. A cold outdoor scene shows the shorter daylight and the children having fun together in the snowy weather. The children are shown enjoying the snow during the short winter day.

pages.text: The snow melts. It gets warmer. Spring comes again.
pages.brief: The snow melts as it gets warmer, and spring comes again; a changing outdoor scene shows the snow disappearing and the warmer spring weather returning to the landscape. The scene marks the end of winter and the fresh return of spring.

pages.text: Children have fun in all seasons!
pages.brief: Children have fun in all seasons. A lively outdoor view shows children enjoying themselves in spring, summer, fall and winter, bringing together the different seasonal scenes from the book. The children are shown having fun and smiling in each season.

books.title: Shapes in Tide Pools
books.art_why: Tide pools, starfish, crabs, snails and mussels all exist today and are photographed in real life.

pages.text: There are pools of water on rocky shores. They are called tide pools. Many animals live in tide pools.
pages.brief: A rocky shore at low tide, with several shallow pools of clear water held between the rocks. Small sea animals are visible inside the pools, some resting on the rocky bottom and sides, others partly hidden among the stones and seaweed at the water's edge.

pages.text: Can you name this animal? This animal has five arms. It is shaped like a star. It is a starfish!
pages.brief: A starfish in a shallow tide pool on a rocky shore. Its five arms spread out around its middle, giving it the shape of a star. It rests on the rock beneath the clear water, surrounded by wet stone and a little seaweed.

pages.text: Can you name this animal? This animal has eight legs and two claws. Its body is shaped like an oval. It is a crab!
pages.brief: A crab standing in a shallow tide pool on rocky shore. Its eight legs spread out to the sides and its two claws are held up in front. Its body is oval shaped, sitting low over the wet rock under the clear water.

pages.text: Can you name this animal? This animal has one foot. It has a shell shaped like a triangle. It is a snail!
pages.brief: A snail in a tide pool on a rocky shore. It moves on its single foot, its soft body pressed to the wet rock. On its back sits a shell shaped like a triangle, with clear water and stone around it.

pages.text: Can you name this animal? This animal lives in a group. It has a shell shaped like an oval. It is a mussel!
pages.brief: A group of mussels crowded together on a rocky shore at the edge of a tide pool. Their shells are oval shaped and packed side by side, attached to the wet rock, with water and more stone around the cluster.

books.title: Places Plants and Animals Live
books.art_why: Real habitats and living things can be photographed.

pages.text: Plants and animals live in the deserts. Deserts are very dry. Deserts can be very hot. Plants and animals live in the oceans. Ocean water is very salty.
pages.brief: A dry, hot desert fills one side of the scene, with sparse plants and small animals living on the dry ground. On the other side, a salty ocean shows water plants and sea animals living in the water.

pages.text: Plants and animals live in the mountains. Mountains are very tall and steep. Plants and animals live in the plains. Plains are very grassy and flat.
pages.brief: Tall, steep mountains rise on one side, with plants and animals living among the slopes. On the other side, flat grassy plains stretch wide, with plants and animals living across the open grassland.

pages.text: Plants and animals live in rivers. River water is not salty. Plants and animals live in rainforests. Rainforests are very wet.
pages.brief: A river flows through a green landscape, with plants and animals living in and beside the fresh water. Nearby, a wet rainforest is thick with plants and animals among dense, leafy growth, and rain falls over the leaves.

pages.text: Plants and animals live in the tundra. The tundra is very cold. The tundra has no trees. Plants and animals live all around the world.
pages.brief: A cold, treeless tundra stretches across the scene, with low plants and small animals living on the frosty ground. A wide view of the world shows plants and animals living in many different places all around the Earth.

books.title: Shoes Men Wear
books.art_why: All eight kinds of shoes are real objects men wear today, so photographs show them clearly.

pages.text: Flip-flops are summer shoes. Men wear them to the beach.
pages.brief: A sunny beach with sand and gentle waves. A man stands near the water wearing flip-flops, his feet and the straps of the sandals clearly visible on the sand. Beside him, a pair of flip-flops rests on a towel. Bright summer sky above, no other people close by.

pages.text: Sneakers are everyday shoes. Men wear them to the park.
pages.brief: A park with green grass and a path. A man walks along the path wearing sneakers, one foot lifted so the shoe and its laces show clearly. Trees and a bench in the background. He looks relaxed, on an ordinary day out, hands loose at his sides.

pages.text: Cleats are sport shoes. Men wear them to play soccer.
pages.brief: A grassy soccer field with a goal in the background. A man in shorts and a jersey runs toward a ball, wearing cleats with studs on the soles. One foot is raised mid-stride so the studded shoe is visible against the grass.

pages.text: Hiking boots are outdoor shoes. Men wear them in the woods.
pages.brief: A woodland trail with tall trees, ferns and rocks. A man in a jacket and small backpack steps over a root, wearing hiking boots. The thick tread and high ankles of the boots show as he lifts one foot onto the uneven ground.

pages.text: Work boots are tough shoes. Men wear them to work.
pages.brief: A work site or workshop with tools and stacked timber. A man in work clothes stands on rough ground wearing tough work boots, the sturdy leather and thick soles clear. He leans slightly forward, steady on his feet, ready for a heavy day of work.

pages.text: Winter boots are warm shoes. Men wear them in the snow.
pages.brief: A snowy street or yard with soft white snow on the ground and falling flakes. A man in a warm coat and hat stands in the snow wearing winter boots, the tall warm shafts and thick soles visible as he leaves footprints behind him.

pages.text: Wingtips are dress shoes. Men wear them to a dance.
pages.brief: A dance floor in a hall with soft lights in the background. A man in a suit stands with one foot forward, wearing polished wingtip dress shoes, the pointed toes and fine punched patterns clearly shown on the shiny leather.

pages.text: Slippers are soft shoes. Men wear them around the house to rest their feet after a busy day.
pages.brief: A cozy living room with a soft armchair and a rug. A man sits back in the chair, feet up, wearing soft slippers. His shoulders are relaxed and his head rests back after a busy day, resting his feet at home.

books.title: Country Animals
books.art_why: Real country animals and outdoor places exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Some people live in the country. Many kinds of animals live in the country, too.
pages.brief: A wide countryside view shows some people living in a rural place while many different kinds of animals are also present nearby, sharing the country setting. The people and animals are all outdoors in the same natural landscape.

pages.text: Deer live in the country. They eat twigs from trees.
pages.brief: In a country setting, several deer stand near trees and eat twigs growing from the branches. The deer are outdoors among the trees, feeding on the twigs in their rural habitat. The scene shows the deer in the country, with trees around them as they eat twigs.

pages.text: Robins live in the country. They make nests in trees.
pages.brief: Robins live in the country, and they make nests in trees. A robin is shown in a tree with its nest, while other trees stand around in the rural setting. The birds are outdoors in the country, building and using nests among the tree branches.

pages.text: Squirrels live in the country. They eat nuts from trees.
pages.brief: Squirrels live in the country, and they eat nuts from trees. A squirrel is shown in a tree holding or eating nuts, with tree branches around it in the rural outdoor setting. The scene is outdoors in the country among trees.

pages.text: Geese and ducks live in the country. They swim in lakes.
pages.brief: Geese and ducks live in the country, and they swim in lakes. The scene shows geese and ducks together on a lake, floating and swimming in the water in a rural outdoor setting. The birds are outdoors on the lake.

pages.text: Raccoons live in the country. They wash their food in rivers.
pages.brief: Raccoons live in the country, and they wash their food in rivers. A raccoon is shown beside or in a river, washing food in the water, with the river and rural outdoor setting around it.

pages.text: Foxes live in the country. They run and play in fields.
pages.brief: Foxes live in the country, and they run and play in fields. The scene shows foxes running and playing outdoors in a grassy field, with the open country field around them. The animals are active in the field.

pages.text: Cows live in the country. They eat grass from fields.
pages.brief: Cows live in the country, and they eat grass from fields. The scene shows cows standing in a field and eating grass, with the open rural field around them in the country. The cows are outdoors in the field.

pages.text: Mice live in the country. They eat grains from fields.
pages.brief: Mice live in the country, and they eat grains from fields. The scene shows mice in a field eating grains, with the outdoor rural field around them as they feed in the country. The mice are small in the field.

pages.text: Do you see animals where you live? What kinds of animals do you see?
pages.brief: A child stands in the place where they live and looks around at animals nearby, inviting the viewer to notice what kinds of animals can be seen in their own local area. The scene asks which animals are there.
